summary: Mentally adding or subtracting multiples of ten to a three-digit number extends the '10 more/less' idea one column up: usually only the tens digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a hundred, in which case the hundreds digit also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and ones, reuse decade facts in the tens (e.g. 7 tens ± some tens), and use make-ten at the scale of tens when crossing a hundred. Teach with a place-value chart and a number line marked in tens around the nearest hundred, deliberately contrasting non-bridging and bridging cases so the exception is visible.
misconceptions: Changing the ones digit instead of the tens (345+40 given as 349)
Failing to bridge a hundred: 372+40 given as 3(11)2 or keeping the tens at 11
Smaller-from-larger in the tens when subtracting bridges down (a hundred not decomposed)
Believing 'only the tens digit ever changes', so bridging-a-hundred cases are mishandled

activities.title: Contrast a non-bridging and a bridging case on a place-value chart
steps: Start with 345 on a place-value chart and add 40 mentally: before calculating, predict which digits will change and which will stay the same.
Confirm that only the tens change (4 tens + 4 tens = 8 tens), giving 385, with the hundreds (3) and ones (5) unchanged.
Now try 372 + 40, again predicting first: notice the tens reach eleven, so a hundred is composed and the hundreds digit ticks up — resolve to 412 (reach 400 by adding 28, then add the remaining 12).
Say aloud how 372 + 40 is like 7 tens + 4 tens = 11 tens, and point to where the extra hundred comes from.
activities.insight: Adding or subtracting tens changes only the tens digit UNLESS the running total of tens crosses a hundred, in which case a hundred is composed (or decomposed) and the hundreds digit changes too — the same kind of exception children already met when crossing a ten.

activities.title: Bridge a hundred downwards when subtracting
steps: Work out 431 − 50 mentally, first predicting whether the hundreds digit will change.
Check the size: subtracting 50 should make the answer exactly 50 less than 431, which takes it below 400. Is your answer below 400, and does adding 50 back give 431?
Use a number line marked in tens to show the jump crosses below 400 (431 − 31 = 400, then − 19 more = 381).
If using base-ten blocks, decompose one hundred into ten tens before removing five tens.
activities.insight: Subtracting tens can bridge a hundred downwards, decomposing a hundred into ten tens; the hundreds digit then decreases, and the result must be smaller than the start.

activities.title: Predict and sort: will the hundreds digit change?
steps: For a mixed set of items (e.g. 345 + 40, 372 + 40, 462 − 30, 431 − 50), predict for each whether the hundreds digit will change before calculating.
Sort the items into 'bridges a hundred' and 'does not bridge a hundred'.
Calculate each mentally, then check your sort against the answers (385, 412, 432, 381).
Explain in your own words the rule: only the tens change unless the calculation crosses a hundred.
activities.insight: Deciding in advance whether a calculation bridges a hundred builds the discriminating judgement that prevents the over-generalisation 'only the tens digit ever changes'.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 40, then 372 + 40, then 431 − 50. After each, ask which digits changed. Watch the two that cross a hundred.
checkAnswer: 385, 412, 381. 345+40 changes only the tens (385). 372+40 bridges a hundred: tens go 7→9 then over, +12 in tens = 412 (hundreds digit changes). 431−50 bridges down: 431−31 to 400, then −19 more = 381 (hundreds digit changes).
